responseText: {"title":"Letters Among the Marks","question":"How does a readable sign change the way we look?","introduction":"Across these fourteen works, words and symbols appear on the same surface as faces, figures, and dense mark-making. Sometimes a word names what we see; sometimes it sits inside a body or floats as pure shape. This exhibition traces what happens at that boundary — where reading and looking pull in different directions, and neither fully wins.","closing":"Each work places a legible sign inside a field of marks that resist easy reading. Whether that tension resolves, or simply holds, is a question each visitor answers differently.","chapters":[{"title":"The Word Inside the Body","introduction":"Three works carry explicit text — a word printed through a figure, a declaration beside one, and two stacked labels framing a collision of marks. Each treats language as material rather than caption.","stops":[{"slot":"W017","whyHere":"'BULLISH' floats semi-transparently through the bear figure's torso, absorbed into the body rather than labeling it from outside.","transitionFromPrevious":null},{"slot":"W060","whyHere":"'STILL BULLISH @NIFTYINK' sits in solid outlined letters apart from the loose mark-making of the dark figure beside it — declaration versus dissolution.","transitionFromPrevious":"Both works carry the same word, but here it shifts from transparent overlay to hard-edged block text standing separate from the figure it accompanies."},{"slot":"W105","whyHere":"Two red 'BULLISH' blocks anchor opposite corners, holding a dense interior of colliding marks and looping lines between them like brackets around noise.","transitionFromPrevious":"The single word now doubles, framing the composition top and bottom rather than inhabiting a figure — text as structural device rather than label."}]},{"title":"Signs That Behave as Shapes","introduction":"These works carry marks that look like writing or symbols but resist full decoding — crowns, spirals, cross-hatching, and lettered fragments that function as visual weight rather than readable content.","stops":[{"slot":"W039","whyHere":"Crown shapes with spirals, blue blocks, and a lime-green oval chain compete as visual events; no single mark resolves into plain meaning.","transitionFromPrevious":"The explicit word disappears; what remains are symbol-like forms — crowns, spirals, grids — that carry the look of significance without delivering a readable message."},{"slot":"W187","whyHere":"White hand-lettered marks run across the mid-section but remain illegible as text, functioning instead as horizontal rhythm against the cross-hatched lower quadrant.","transitionFromPrevious":"Both works layer mark types across a busy field, but here a face structure organizes the chaos — X-marked eyes and an open mouth hold the center while marks compete around them."},{"slot":"W264","whyHere":"Loose lettering fills the top band in the same thick outline style as the central forms, making text and image indistinguishable in visual weight.","transitionFromPrevious":"The face structure becomes more schematic — two eye-like forms, one a spiral and one a rectangle, sit side by side, and the lettering above them reads as part of the same drawn system."}]},{"title":"Faces Without Anchors","introduction":"Four works build faces from glowing voids, scribbled masses, and competing color zones — present as figures but refusing the stability that a readable sign might provide.","stops":[{"slot":"W148","whyHere":"Two blown-out light orbs replace eyes entirely, erasing the detail that would anchor expression; the face is present but not fully legible.","transitionFromPrevious":"After works dense with competing marks, this face strips back to near-darkness — the scribbled mass above and looping jaw below hold a figure together without resolving it."},{"slot":"W165","whyHere":"Stitched seam lines and bared teeth give the figure visible structure, but the fractured hat and uneven background glow keep it from settling into a stable read.","transitionFromPrevious":"Where the previous face dissolved into light and dark, this one is assembled — seams, teeth, and a layered hat — yet the parts refuse to cohere into a single mood."},{"slot":"W186","whyHere":"Coiled white rows, red spikes, and a hard white wedge fill the rounded form's interior, holding the image between a face and something else entirely.","transitionFromPrevious":"The stitched assembly gives way to a form whose interior splits into competing zones — the coiled lower section reads as teeth or grin, but no dark opening confirms it."},{"slot":"W159","whyHere":"Heart shapes appear as both central form and repeated smaller motifs; the jagged white outline keeps the familiar symbol unsettled rather than resolved.","transitionFromPrevious":"The face structure drops away; a recognizable symbol — the heart — takes its place, but the jagged outline and warm dense field give it the same unresolved quality as the faces before it."}]},{"title":"Text as Costume and Broadcast","introduction":"Three works place legible text on or near figures as a kind of worn or projected identity — a labeled cauldron, a chest-tag, and graffiti beside a mechanical face.","stops":[{"slot":"W191","whyHere":"'SCAFFOLD ETH' hand-lettered on the cauldron pulls the silhouetted figure between emblem and joke, ceremony and deflation held in the same image.","transitionFromPrevious":"The heart symbol gives way to a fully legible label — but here the text is on an object the figure bends over, making the word a prop rather than a body marking."},{"slot":"W171","whyHere":"'CCO SUMMER' on a white rectangle at the chest reads as a tag or badge worn by the yellow face, while scattered white marks around the black field read as static.","transitionFromPrevious":"The text moves from object to body — worn as a chest label rather than inscribed on a cauldron — and the figure's blue-framed eyes give it a fixed, outward stare the silhouette lacked."},{"slot":"W279","whyHere":"Graffiti lettering in the lower-left corner sits beside a mechanical face with lens-bar eyes and a barred mouth, treating the text as a second layer of address alongside the figure.","transitionFromPrevious":"The badge becomes graffiti — text that addresses the viewer from outside the figure rather than being worn by it, while the face itself turns more mechanical and less expressive."}]},{"title":"Everything at Once","introduction":"The final two works push every element — motifs, marks, symbols, and assembled parts — to the edges of the frame simultaneously, testing how much a surface can hold.","stops":[{"slot":"W302","whyHere":"Heart-shaped lenses, a target, coil lines, rectangular blocks, and a row of marks at the mouth all compete across the same layer, making the face feel assembled from colliding parts.","transitionFromPrevious":"Where the previous work split text and face into distinct zones, here every element crowds the frame at once — motifs, marks, and structural lines refuse any hierarchy."},{"slot":"W165","whyHere":"Revisited here as contrast: its restrained palette and single stitched figure make the density of the preceding work visible by opposition.","transitionFromPrevious":"After the maximum density of the assembled face, the stitched figure's relative stillness — one form, one ground — sharpens the question of how much a surface needs to carry."}]}]}
